This is second priority because a dead refusal guard hides a security-policy refusal, allowing invalid school-route leases through \u2014 a silent policy bypass rather than record corruption.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the lease-mismatch refusal is purely defensive and no code path can actually produce a mismatched lease in production, the guard is dead code and lower priority than unimported functions.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If an integration test already exercises mismatched leases end-to-end, the gap is covered.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The lease-mismatch refusal is a firewall guard: it blocks requests with inconsistent lease/route metadata. If the guard dies, invalid routing decisions pass undetected. Unlike the digest gap, this does not corrupt stored records \u2014 it silently allows unauthorized or inconsistent routing. The cheapest test: inject a request with a mismatched lease/endpoint pair and assert the firewall raises SCHOOL_ROUTE_LEASE_MISMATCH or SCHOOL_ROUTE_ENDPOINT_MISMATCH. One test function, two assertions (one per error code). Blast radius: a refused-but-should-have-been-accepted request becomes accepted, but existing records remain intact.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
